title: Hitting a Moving Target: Test-Time Adaptation for AI Text Detection under Continual Distribution Shift
claim: Fixed supervised detectors fail once the data distribution shifts; adapting at test time with unlabeled submissions keeps detection robust.
layout: Left: 2 stacked flow rows (top supervised, bottom TTA) with feature-space insets; right: scatter plot
description: The figure has two parts. On the left is a flow diagram split by a horizontal gray line into a supervised row (top) and a semi-supervised test-time adaptation row (bottom). Columns are labeled Training Detector, Distribution shift, Inference Detector, and Feature space. Blue rounded boxes hold the training and inference steps. A central orange box lists three shifts: humanizers, new LLMs, and human writing drift. Orange and blue arrows connect the boxes. In the top row, a red cross marks shifted AI text classified as human. In the bottom row, a green check marks shifted AI classified as AI. Each row ends in a small feature-space inset. Green circles are human text, orange rings are shifted AI, and purple squares are AI. A fixed decision boundary appears on top. On the bottom, the boundary moves after the unlabeled data is added. On the right is an LDA scatter plot with three clusters: human in green, naive AI in purple, and adversarial AI in brown.
caption: (left) Comparing AI text detection with supervised learning (top) and test-time adaptation with semi-supervised learning (bottom). With supervised detection: a detector is trained on labeled human and AI text, released, and can fail under distribution shift. With TTA: the detector re-estimates its boundary using submitted texts at inference time and therefore can adapt. (right) Empirical illustration---human, naive AI, and adversarial AI are all (approximately) mutually separable, but the latter may evade a fixed classifier. Details on figure generation are in [ref].
abstract: Deployed AI text detection approaches are supervised, relying on training-time access to labeled datasets of both human-written and AI-generated text. This approach is vulnerable to three types of distribution shifts that occur continually post-deployment, and for which labeled data is often unavailable: adversarial humanization, new LLMs being released, and unidentifiable temporal drift in human writing after widespread LLM usage. Simultaneously, existing approaches do not leverage a key signal of LLM usage: inference-time homogeneity. We propose a test-time adaptation (TTA) approach that adapts to distribution shifts by leveraging homogeneity among unlabeled samples observed at inference time. Empirically, we find that state-of-the-art supervised detectors systematically fail when they encounter distribution shifts in AI-generated and human writing, both adversarial and natural, while TTA with semi-supervised learning is largely robust; e.g., the commercial model Pangram detects just 27.0% of our adversarial AI-generated text, compared to 93.3% for our test-time approach. We establish that TTA is a promising framework for AI text detection in the wild.
